memory_candidates.content: When retargeting tests after two sibling SKILL.md files are merged into one hard_mode-gated file, do not assume a mechanism previously invoked separately per-engine (e.g. a resolver script call) is still duplicated per-branch in the merged file -- verify by inspection first. In one observed case, a resolver (command-route-agent.sh) that the old base/hard file pair each called separately was consolidated to a SINGLE unconditional call in the merged file's shared preamble (Stage 1b), with both hard_mode branches reading the same resolved variable rather than each re-invoking the resolver. A test written against the old per-engine-call assumption needs adapting to check the resolved variable's dispatch presence inside each branch instead, anchored on each branch's own unique heading text -- this preserves the identical regression-catching property (verified via mutation test) without asserting something that no longer exists.

A mutation check's own assumption ("renaming/deleting X will make the test fail loudly") is itself a claim that must be verified, not assumed -- a test's existing assertions may pattern-match only for their OWN expected substring's presence and never check for absence of unrelated noise (e.g. a bash "command not found" error on stderr from a broken stub-by-name mechanism), so a genuine regression can pass silently even though the mechanism it depends on (a stub function matching a production function's name) is structurally documented as load-bearing. Running the mutation check for real, not just trusting the file's own header comment claiming it's load-bearing, is what surfaces this class of gap -- and the fix is a small, targeted negative assertion (e.g. grep stderr for "command not found"), not a rewrite.

When a plan's acceptance test says a set of N target files must pass "both before and after" a related file's future deletion, actually simulate the deletion (temporary rename, not permanent) and re-run every target file, even when each file already passes independently against the current on-disk state. A target file can depend on an OUT-OF-SCOPE sibling suite (one you are not authorized to modify per the plan's own Non-Goals) whose own preflight independently requires the file being removed -- this coupling is invisible until the removal is actually simulated. The correct fix lives in the in-scope target file's own invocation of the sibling (a narrow, specifically-matched carve-out for that sibling's known, already-documented limitation), not in the out-of-scope sibling itself.
